chapters.title: Equip and Edify
chapters.subtitle: Mending nets and building houses: how God makes his people ready
chapters.trueMeaning: mend, fit out, and build up
chapters.nutshell: In church English, “equip” can sound like a training course and “edify” like a pleasant feeling. The Greek word behind “equip” was used for mending fishing nets and restoring what is broken, and “edify” simply means “to build a house”. Hebrew thinks the same way: God builds, establishes and strengthens his people, as he filled Bezalel with skill to build his dwelling.
chapters.bigIdea: God equips his people the way a fisherman mends his nets and a builder raises a house: repairing what is torn, fitting each part for its work, and building everyone together into one dwelling for him.
skeleton: We often hear “equip” as training and “edify” as feeling inspired.
Katartizō means to put in order: mend nets, restore a person, fit out completely.
Ephesians 4:12 says leaders equip the saints so that all of them do the work of ministry.
Oikodomē, “edification”, is house-building; the church is God's building.
Hebrew banah (build), kun (establish) and chazaq (strengthen) give the same picture.
Bezalel was filled with God's Spirit and practical skill to build the Tabernacle.
Older translations said “perfecting” and “edifying” after the Latin; modern ones say “equip” and “build up”.
Equipping is shared, practical, patient with the broken, and aimed at love.

p: When churches talk about **equipping**, we often picture a seminar, a course or a toolkit. **Edify** sounds even more distant: an old church word for something that makes you feel uplifted or teaches you a nice lesson. Many people assume that equipping is the job of trained leaders, and that being edified is something that happens to you while you sit and listen to a good sermon.

The words behind these English terms are much more down to earth. One was used by fishermen mending their nets and, in Greek medical writing, for setting a limb back in place. The other simply means **building a house**. In the Hebrew Bible, God himself is the builder who establishes and strengthens his people. Seeing these pictures changes how we think about church: it is a workshop and a building site, not only an audience.

The main Greek verb is *katartizō*. Its basic idea is **to put something in proper order** so that it can do its job. In Mark 1:19 Jesus sees James and John in their boat “mending the nets”. Those nets had been torn by rocks and heavy catches, and the brothers were repairing them so they would be ready for the next night's fishing. That ordinary, patient task is *katartizō*.

Paul uses the same verb for people: “if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should **restore** him in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1). The picture is repair, not punishment. Greek medical writers could use this word family for setting a dislocated joint back in place: painful for a moment, but done so that the body can work again.

Elsewhere *katartizō* means to make complete or fully ready. A disciple who is “fully trained” will be like his teacher (Luke 6:40). Peter promises that after suffering God will “restore, confirm, strengthen and establish you” (1 Peter 5:10). Hebrews prays that God will “equip you with everything good that you may do his will” (Hebrews 13:21), and even says the universe was “framed”, put in order, by the word of God (Hebrews 11:3).

The noun *katartismos* appears only once in the New Testament. Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers “to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:11–12). Leaders mend and fit out God's people; then **the people themselves do the work of ministry**, and the whole body is built up.

A related verb, *exartizō*, appears in 2 Timothy 3:17: Scripture is given “that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work”. Both words describe being fitted out fully for a task. The goal is not knowledge stored in the head but good work done with the hands, and a body that grows “so that it builds itself up in love” (Ephesians 4:16).

*Oikodomē* is made from *oikos*, “house”, and a root meaning “to build”. In the Gospels it is ordinary building language: the wise man “built his house on the rock” (Matthew 7:24), and Jesus says, “I will build my church” (Matthew 16:18). Paul applies the word to people: “you are God's field, God's building” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

In 1 Corinthians 14 he tests every gift in worship by one question: does it build up the church? The one who prophesies speaks to people “for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation” (14:3), and “let all things be done for building up” (14:26). “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (8:1). So he urges, “encourage one another and build one another up” (1 Thessalonians 5:11).
> Edification in the Bible is not a private feeling of being inspired. It is a wall going up stone by stone: something you can see in a community that grows stronger, kinder and more united.

The Hebrew word for build is *banah*. God “built” the rib he took from the man into a woman (Genesis 2:22). Rachel and Leah “built the house of Israel” by bearing children (Ruth 4:11), and God promises to “build a house” for David, meaning a family line (2 Samuel 7:27). When Sarai gives Hagar to Abram she says, literally, “perhaps I shall be built through her” (Genesis 16:2). In Hebrew, building is about people and families as much as stones.

Jewish tradition links *banah* with *ben*, “son”, and *banim*, “children”; linguists debate whether the words truly share a root, but the link is old. The Talmud reads Isaiah 54:13, “great shall be the peace of your children (*banayikh*)”, and says: do not read “your children” but “your builders” (*bonayikh*), because students of Torah increase peace in the world (Talmud Berakhot 64a).

Two more words complete the picture. *Kun* means to stand firm, establish or prepare: “establish the work of our hands” (Psalm 90:17). *Chazaq* means to be strong or to strengthen: “be strong and courageous” (Joshua 1:6–9). When Nehemiah called the people to rebuild Jerusalem's walls, they answered, “Let us rise up and build”, and “they strengthened their hands for the good work” (Nehemiah 2:18). Building and strengthening go together.

sections.h: Bezalel: filled to build God's dwelling
p: The first person the Bible names as “filled with the Spirit of God” is not a prophet or a priest but a craftsman. God says of Bezalel, “I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship, to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver and bronze” (Exodus 31:3–4). He and Oholiab were equipped to build the Tabernacle, the place where God would dwell among his people.

The word translated “ability” is *chokhmah*, the Bible's usual word for wisdom. Here it plainly means practical skill. Exodus 35:34 adds that God put it in Bezalel's heart **to teach** others. Equipping in the Bible is passed on: the skilled train the willing, and God's Spirit equips hands as well as hearts and lips.

Priests were made ready in another way. The Hebrew idiom for ordaining a priest is “to fill his hand” (*mille yad*), as in Exodus 28:41, where English versions say “ordain” or “consecrate”. At the priests' installation, portions of the offering were placed in their hands (Leviticus 8:27). Being equipped for God's work meant receiving something to carry and to offer.

Older English Bibles followed the Latin tradition here. The Latin Vulgate renders Ephesians 4:12 *ad consummationem sanctorum*, “for the completing of the saints”, and the King James Version says “for the **perfecting** of the saints”. That was a fair choice, because *katartizō* can mean to make complete. But in modern English “perfect” suggests flawless, and the picture of mending and fitting out is lost. The ESV, NASB and NIV say “to equip the saints”, which is closer to everyday usage.

The KJV also places commas between three phrases: “for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ”. Read that way, all three jobs belong to the leaders. Most modern versions read the Greek so that leaders equip the saints, and the saints do the work of ministry. Scholars still discuss the grammar, but both readings agree that the whole body is to be built up.

“Edify” comes from Latin *aedificare*, from *aedes* (a dwelling or temple) and *facere* (to make). In 1611 “edify one another” (KJV) was a good match, because readers still heard the building in it, as in “edifice”. Since then “edifying” has come to mean morally improving or simply pleasant, so the ESV and NIV usually say “build up”. And because translators rightly vary *katartizō* by context (mend, restore, fully trained, perfect, equip, frame), English readers cannot see that one verb runs from the fishing boat to the church.

In Galilee, fishing was a family business. Zebedee's sons worked with their father and hired men (Mark 1:20). They fished at night with large nets and spent the morning washing and mending them (Luke 5:2). A torn net lets the catch escape, so mending was daily, patient, skilled work. When Jesus called fishermen to become “fishers of people”, he called men who already knew that equipment must be kept in good repair.

Building was everywhere in Jesus' world. Herod's rebuilding of the Temple had been going on for forty-six years (John 2:20), and Jesus himself is called a *tektōn*, a builder or craftsman (Mark 6:3). In Greek and Roman cities, wealthy citizens won honour by paying for public buildings and putting their names on them. Paul turns this around: in the church, honour goes to whoever builds others up, and even the weakest members are indispensable (1 Corinthians 12:22–25).

Jews also knew that a community could be God's dwelling. The Psalms speak of the LORD building up Zion (Psalm 102:16), and some Jewish groups of the time, such as the community behind the Dead Sea Scrolls, described their fellowship as a kind of holy house. The apostles say that believers together are “a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:21) and “living stones… being built up as a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:5).

Equipping starts with **repair**. Before people can serve, the torn places in their lives often need gentle mending, as Galatians 6:1 says. A church that equips is patient with the broken and never quick to throw away a torn net. Ask God to make you someone who restores others gently rather than someone who exposes them.

Equipping is also **shared**. Leaders are given to fit out the saints, and the saints do the ministry. Ask: what is my part in building others up this week? A word of encouragement, a skill taught, a meal shared, a burden carried. Test what you do in worship and in conversation by Paul's question: does it build up?

> When Jewish congregations finish reading one of the five books of the Torah, they call out together, “*Chazak, chazak, venitchazek*”: “Be strong, be strong, and let us strengthen one another.” That is edification in one line.

words.note: Used for houses, cities and families; God “built” the woman from the rib.
words.missed: “Made” (Genesis 2:22) or “obtain children” (Genesis 16:2) hides that the Hebrew says “build”.
words.culture: In Israel a “house” meant a family line as well as a building, so having children was “building a house”.

words.note: Pictures something set firmly in place so that it stands.
words.missed: Translated establish, prepare, order or direct, so readers miss the single picture of firm footing.
words.culture: Builders set posts and foundations firmly; a king's throne and a person's steps are “established” the same way.

words.note: Often said to encourage someone for a task.
words.missed: “Be strong” can sound like private willpower; in Hebrew it is usually encouragement for shared work.
words.culture: Jewish congregations say “Chazak, chazak, venitchazek” when they finish reading a book of the Torah.

words.gloss: to fill the hand: to ordain
words.note: The idiom for equipping a priest for his service.
words.missed: “Ordain” or “consecrate” sounds like a ceremony; the Hebrew pictures hands filled with something to offer.
words.culture: At the priests' installation, portions of the offering were placed in their hands.

words.note: In Bezalel's story it means practical craftsmanship given by God's Spirit.
words.missed: “Wisdom” suggests ideas; here it is skill with gold, wood, stone and cloth.
words.culture: Craftsmen in Israel trained apprentices; Bezalel was also given the gift to teach (Exodus 35:34).

words.gloss: to mend, restore, put in order, equip
words.note: From mending nets to restoring people and making them fully ready.
words.missed: Rendered “mend”, “restore”, “perfect” and “equip” in different verses, so English hides the one word linking them.
words.culture: Galilean fishermen mended nets every morning; Greek doctors could use the word family for setting joints.

words.note: Leaders equip the saints so that the saints do the work of ministry.
words.missed: KJV “perfecting”, following the Latin, now sounds like flawlessness rather than readiness for work.
words.culture: A mended, folded net is ready for the next night's fishing; equipped saints are ready to serve.

words.note: Scripture fits God's servant out completely for every good work.
words.missed: “Thoroughly furnished” (KJV) can sound like furniture; the idea is fully fitted out for a job.
words.culture: In ordinary Greek the word family described things fitted out and ready for use.

words.note: Literally house-building; Paul's test for every gift in worship.
words.missed: “Edification” now sounds like a pleasant feeling or a moral lesson; the Greek is a building going up.
words.culture: Greek benefactors won honour by funding buildings; Paul gives that honour to anyone who builds others up.

words.note: The same verb for building a house and strengthening one another.
words.missed: When versions say “build” in the Gospels and “edify” in the letters, readers miss that it is one word.
words.culture: Jesus is called a builder or craftsman (Mark 6:3), and Herod's Temple was being built throughout his life.

rows.literal: for the mending and fitting-out of the holy ones
rows.common: for the perfecting of the saints (KJV)
rows.why: “Perfecting” follows the Latin consummatio and was fair in 1611, but today it suggests flawlessness and hides the picture of being made ready for work.
“Mending” is exactly right here, but because Ephesians uses “equip”, readers never see that it is the same verb.

rows.literal: set such a person right again
rows.why: “Restore” is a good choice; the Greek adds the picture of repairing a net or resetting a joint, gently and with skill.
“Edify” comes from Latin aedificare, “to build”, but the building picture has faded from the English word, so the ESV and NIV say “build one another up”.

rows.literal: and the LORD God built the rib (into a woman)
rows.why: “Made” reads more naturally in English, but the Hebrew “built” connects the first woman to the building of houses and families.

steps.d: A net is torn; a person stumbles into sin (Galatians 6:1).
Gently restored and set back in order (katartizō).
Equipped for every good work by Scripture and gifts (2 Timothy 3:17).
Every saint does the work of ministry (Ephesians 4:12).
The body builds itself up in love (Ephesians 4:16).

verses.text: He saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who were in their boat mending the nets.
If anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness.
He gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers, to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ.
…that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.
I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship.
They said, “Let us rise up and build.” So they strengthened their hands for the good work.

keyPoints: Katartizō means to put in order: the same verb is used for mending nets (Mark 1:19), restoring a person (Galatians 6:1) and equipping for good works (Hebrews 13:21).
Leaders are given to equip the saints, and the saints do the work of ministry (Ephesians 4:12).
“Edify” means to build a house; Paul tests every gift by whether it builds up the church (1 Corinthians 14:26).
Hebrew banah (build) is used of families as well as houses; God “built” the woman (Genesis 2:22).
Bezalel, the first person the Bible names as filled with the Spirit of God, was equipped with practical skill and the gift to teach.
“Perfecting” and “edifying” come from the Latin tradition; “equip” and “build up” recover the everyday pictures.
Building up is shared work done in love, not a private feeling.
reflect: Is there a “torn net” in someone's life that you could help to mend gently this week?
What practical skill has God given you, and how could you use it to build others up or teach someone else?
When you leave a gathering of believers, do you ask only “Was I blessed?” or also “Did I build someone up?”

quiz.q: In Mark 1:19, what were James and John doing with the verb katartizō?
quiz.why: They were mending, putting in order, their nets: the same verb Paul uses for restoring and equipping people.

quiz.q: According to Ephesians 4:12 (as most modern versions read it), who does the work of ministry?
options: No one; it is God's work alone
quiz.why: Leaders equip the saints, and the saints themselves do the work of ministry so the body is built up.

quiz.q: What does the Greek word oikodomē (edification) literally mean?
quiz.why: It comes from oikos, “house”, and building; edifying means building others up.

quiz.q: What does Genesis 2:22 literally say God did with the rib?
options: He built it into a woman
quiz.why: The Hebrew verb is banah, “build”; most English versions say “made”.

quiz.q: Who is the first person the Bible names as “filled with the Spirit of God”?
quiz.why: Exodus 31:3 says God filled Bezalel with his Spirit and with skill to build the Tabernacle.

terms.def: To put in order: mend, restore, make complete, equip.
Equipping or fitting out; used once, in Ephesians 4:12.
Building or building up; the word behind “edification”.
Hebrew “to build”, used of houses, cities and families.
Hebrew “to be strong, to strengthen”; often an encouragement for a task.
“To fill the hand”, the Hebrew idiom for ordaining a priest.
The Latin Bible used in the Western church for over a thousand years; it shaped many English church words.

chapters.title: Aim, Goal and “Missing the Mark”
chapters.subtitle: Slingers, archers and runners: the Bible's words for sin and for the goal we were made for
chapters.trueMeaning: missing the goal God set for us
chapters.nutshell: The Bible's most common words for sin, Hebrew chata and Greek hamartanō, can both mean simply “to miss”: a slinger missing his target, a traveller missing the way. Other words picture sin as twisting something straight, breaking faith, or straying by mistake. To see sin clearly we also need the goal: the Greek words skopos and telos point to the target God has set before us, which is love and likeness to Christ.
chapters.bigIdea: Sin is not only breaking rules but missing, twisting or rebelling against the good goal God made us for, and the gospel puts us back on course toward that goal.
skeleton: In English “sin” sounds like breaking a rule, and “missing the mark” can sound minor.
Hebrew chata means to miss: the slingers of Judges 20:16 “would not miss”.
Avon pictures twisting, pesha a breach of loyalty, and shagah straying by mistake.
The three main words appear together in Exodus 34:7 and in the high priest's confession.
Greek hamartanō also meant to miss; the Septuagint used it for chata.
Paraptōma is a false step and anomia is lawlessness.
Skopos and telos name the target: Christ, love and the upward call.
Translators chose “sin”, “iniquity” and “trespass”; the pictures behind them help us repent and aim again.

p: For many people, **sin** means breaking a rule: a list of things you must not do. Others have heard that the Greek word for sin means “missing the mark”, and conclude that sin is just a near miss, an honest mistake that is not very serious. Both ideas hold some truth, and both miss something important.

The Bible uses a whole family of words for what goes wrong in human life. Some picture **missing a target** or losing the way. Others picture **twisting** what was straight, **breaking faith** with a king or friend, or **straying** by accident. And to understand missing a target, we also need to know what the target is. This study looks at both: the words for sin, and the words for the goal.

sections.h: Chata: the slinger who does not miss
p: The most common Hebrew verb for sin is *chata*. Its everyday meaning appears in Judges 20:16: seven hundred left-handed men of Benjamin “could sling a stone at a hair and not miss”. The word for “miss” is *chata*. A traveller who rushes may also *chata*: “whoever makes haste with his feet misses his way” (Proverbs 19:2, ESV). In Job 5:24 the man at peace will look over his fold and “miss nothing”.

From this verb come the nouns *chet* and *chatta'ah*, “sin”. *Chatta'ah* is also the name of an offering (Leviticus 4), often called the “sin offering” but better understood as a **purification offering**, because it cleansed the sanctuary from the stain of sin. Remarkably, the same verb in another form means to purify: David prays, “purge me with hyssop” (Psalm 51:7), literally “de-sin me”. Missing the mark is real, but God provides a way to be cleansed and to aim again.

sections.h: Avon, pesha and shagah: twisted, broken, astray
p: *Avon*, usually translated “iniquity”, is generally connected with a root meaning **to bend or twist**. In Lamentations 3:9 God “has made my paths crooked” using this root. *Avon* covers the twisted act, the guilt it brings, and its painful consequence: Cain says, “my *avon* is greater than I can bear” (Genesis 4:13), meaning his punishment as much as his guilt.

*Pesha*, often “transgression”, is the language of politics and broken trust. “Israel rebelled (*pasha*) against the house of David” (1 Kings 12:19), and Edom “revolted” from Judah (2 Kings 8:20). *Pesha* is a breach of loyalty, like a subject turning against his king or a friend betraying a covenant. “I reared children… but they have rebelled against me” (Isaiah 1:2).

*Shagah* means **to stray or wander**, like a sheep that drifts off. Leviticus 4:2 speaks of a person who sins *bishgagah*, “unintentionally”. The Torah treats these sins differently from sins done “with a high hand”, in open defiance (Numbers 15:27–31). The Psalmist prays both “let me not wander from your commandments” (Psalm 119:10) and “who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults” (Psalm 19:12).

When God reveals his name to Moses he is the God who forgives “iniquity and transgression and sin” (Exodus 34:7): *avon*, *pesha* and *chatta'ah*. On the Day of Atonement the high priest laid his hands on the goat and confessed over it “all the iniquities of the people of Israel, and all their transgressions, all their sins” (Leviticus 16:21). The three words together mean every kind of wrong.

The Mishnah records the high priest's confession using all three verbs (Mishnah Yoma 3:8), and the Talmud discusses their meaning and order: *chet* for unintentional sins, *avon* for deliberate ones, and *pesha* for rebellious ones (Talmud Yoma 36b). Jewish confession on Yom Kippur still lists sins by many names, in the plural: “*Al chet shechatanu*”, “for the sin which we have sinned before you”.
> Hebrew does not have one flat word for sin. It has a vocabulary as rich as human failure: missing, twisting, betraying, straying. And for each one, the same God offers forgiveness.

sections.h: Greek words: missing, false steps and lawlessness
p: The main Greek verb is *hamartanō*, with the noun *hamartia*. In older Greek it could mean to miss a target with a spear or arrow, or more generally to fail or go wrong. The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, chose this word family for *chata*, and in Judges 20:16 it uses a compound of the same verb for the slingers who did not miss. By New Testament times *hamartia* was simply the ordinary word for sin, so we should not press the archery picture into every verse.

*Paraptōma* means a **false step**, a slip or fall beside the path. It is the word behind “trespasses” in Matthew 6:14–15 and Ephesians 2:1, and in Galatians 6:1, “if anyone is caught in any transgression”. *Anomia* means **lawlessness**, living as if there were no Torah at all: “sin is lawlessness” (1 John 3:4). Jesus warns those who call him “Lord” but practise *anomia* (Matthew 7:23). The Septuagint often uses *anomia* for Hebrew *avon*.

sections.h: Skopos and telos: the target and the goal
p: You cannot miss a mark without a mark. Paul names it: “I press on toward the **goal** (*skopos*) for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:14). A *skopos* was something you fix your eyes on, a marker or target. Paul pictures a runner who forgets what lies behind, strains forward, and keeps his eyes on the finishing line.

*Telos* means end, goal or purpose: the point something is aiming at. “The aim (*telos*) of our charge is love from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith” (1 Timothy 1:5). In Romans 10:4 “Christ is the *telos* of the law”; scholars debate whether this means the law's end, its goal, or both, and many think “goal” is central. The related word *teleios*, “complete, mature”, appears in “you therefore must be perfect” (Matthew 5:48).

Paul joins the two pictures in Romans 3:23: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” Humans were made in God's image to reflect his glory. Sin is falling short of that goal, like an arrow dropping before it reaches the target. The good news is that God does not change the target; he restores the archer.

English has no single word that means both “miss” and “sin”, so translators must choose. In Judges 20:16 every major version (KJV, ESV, NIV) rightly says “miss”, and in most other places they say “sin”. That is correct, but readers never see that the same Hebrew word is behind both. The ESV keeps the picture in Proverbs 19:2, “misses his way”, while the KJV has “sinneth”.

“Iniquity” for *avon* comes through Latin *iniquitas*, from *in-* (not) and *aequus* (level, even): unevenness, crookedness. In 1611 that was a fine match for “twisted”, but today “iniquity” is a church word that few people use. The NIV often prefers “sin”, “wickedness” or “guilt” for readability, which loses the difference between the words. “Trespass” for *paraptōma* (KJV, ESV in Ephesians 2:1) once meant stepping across a line; today many readers think of private property signs.

In 1 John 3:4 the KJV says “sin is the transgression of the law”, while the ESV, NIV and NASB say “sin is lawlessness”. The older wording made sense in a tradition that focused on law-keeping; the newer wording is closer to *anomia*, which pictures a life with no law at all. Finally, Philippians 3:14 in the KJV, “I press toward the **mark**”, keeps the target picture, while modern versions say “goal”, which is clearer but less vivid.

Ancient Israel had skilled slingers and archers. Shepherds like David used the sling to protect their flocks, and armies used it in battle. Jonathan shot arrows past a target as a signal to David (1 Samuel 20:20–22). Lamentations even pictures God setting up a person “as a target for his arrow” (3:12). When an Israelite heard *chata*, he could hear the everyday world of aiming and missing, and of walking a road and losing the way.

*Pesha* comes from the world of kings and covenants, where loyalty was everything and rebellion was shameful betrayal. In a culture of honour and shame, sin is not only a broken rule but a broken relationship that dishonours the one who was trusted. That is why confession in Israel was public and communal.

In the Greek world, Paul's readers knew the athletic games: the Olympic and Isthmian Games (the Isthmian Games were held near Corinth). Runners fixed their eyes on the turning post or finish, and the winner received a wreath (1 Corinthians 9:24–27). *Skopos* and *telos* came naturally to people who watched races and archery contests. Paul uses that world to say: keep your eyes on Christ.

Name sin honestly, with the Bible's full vocabulary. Some of our failures are missed shots; some are twisted desires; some are open rebellion; some are things we did not even notice. Jewish confession teaches us to name them all, and to say “we”, because we fail together and are restored together.

Then look at the target. Sin is defined by the goal: love from a pure heart, the glory of God, the upward call in Christ. Repentance (*teshuvah*, turning) is not only feeling sorry but turning back to aim again. God, who purifies and forgives, restores the archer and sets him back on the path.
> “One thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal” (Philippians 3:13–14).

words.note: The everyday word for missing a target or the way, and the most common word for sin.
words.missed: English must choose “miss” or “sin”, so readers never see that one word stands behind both.
words.culture: Slingers, archers and travellers on hill roads knew what it was to hit or miss.

words.note: The same word names sin and the offering that cleansed from it.
words.missed: “Sin offering” hides that its main work was purifying the sanctuary.
words.culture: Brought to the Tabernacle or Temple when someone sinned unintentionally.

words.note: Used in the Yom Kippur confession “Al chet”.
words.missed: Translated simply “sin”, losing the picture of a miss.
words.culture: Jews confess “Al chet shechatanu”, “for the sin we have sinned”, in the plural.

words.note: Usually linked to a root meaning “bend, twist”.
words.missed: “Iniquity” is now an old church word, and the sense of twisted path and its consequence is lost.
words.culture: Israel saw guilt as a weight that a person carries until God lifts it (Psalm 38:4).

words.note: Political language for breaking loyalty with a king or covenant partner.
words.missed: “Transgression” sounds like crossing a legal line; the Hebrew is betrayal of a relationship.
words.culture: In a world of kings and treaties, rebellion was the deepest shame.

words.note: Wandering off course, often without realising it.
words.missed: “Sin through ignorance” (KJV) can sound like no fault at all; the Torah still provided cleansing.
words.culture: Shepherds knew sheep that drift away while grazing, not out of rebellion.

words.note: In older Greek it could mean missing a target; the Septuagint used it for chata.
words.missed: By New Testament times it simply meant “sin”, so the archery picture should not be overpressed.
words.culture: Greek audiences knew javelin and archery contests at the games.

words.note: The ordinary New Testament word for sin, both acts and a power.
words.missed: Paul often speaks of hamartia as a ruling power, not only single acts; “sins” in English can hide this.
words.culture: In Greek drama hamartia could mean a fatal error; in the Bible it is failure before God.

words.note: A slip or fall beside the path.
words.missed: “Trespass” today suggests private property signs rather than a fall.
words.culture: Travellers on rough paths knew the danger of one false step.

words.note: Living as if God had given no Torah; often used in the Septuagint for avon.
words.missed: KJV “transgression of the law” makes it one broken rule; the Greek is a lawless life.
words.culture: For Jews, the Torah was a gift that shaped a people; to be without it was to be lost.

words.note: The mark the runner fixes his eyes on.
words.missed: “Goal” is clear but loses the picture of a target you look at.
words.culture: Runners at the Greek games fixed their eyes on the post at the end of the track.

words.note: The point something aims at; it can mean both finish and fulfilment.
words.missed: “End” can sound like “stop”, when the word often means “goal” or “aim”.
words.culture: Greek thinkers asked what each thing's telos was; Paul answers: love, and Christ.

rows.literal: slinging a stone at a hair and not missing
rows.common: sling stones at an hair breadth, and not miss (KJV)
rows.why: Here every version rightly says “miss”, which shows the everyday meaning hidden elsewhere behind “sin”.

rows.literal: one who hurries with his feet misses (the way)
rows.common: he that hasteth with his feet sinneth (KJV)
rows.why: The KJV used its normal word “sin”; the ESV's “misses his way” recovers the traveller's picture.

rows.original: πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον καὶ ὑστεροῦνται τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ
rows.literal: all missed and are lacking the glory of God
rows.common: all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God (KJV)
rows.why: “Come short” keeps the picture of falling short of a goal; the goal is God's glory that we were made to reflect.
Modern versions say “goal” for clarity; the KJV's “mark” keeps the image of a fixed target.

rows.common: sin is the transgression of the law (KJV)
rows.why: The KJV explains the word as breaking a rule; the ESV and NIV “lawlessness” keeps the sense of living as if there were no law.

diagrams.title: From straying to rebellion
diagrams.note: The Torah and the rabbis distinguished kinds of wrong, but God offers forgiveness for all of them (Exodus 34:7).

verses.text: Every one could sling a stone at a hair and not miss.
…keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin.
Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin!
Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults.
For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.
The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith.

keyPoints: Hebrew chata and Greek hamartanō can both mean “to miss”: a target or the way.
Avon pictures twisting, pesha a breach of loyalty, shagah straying unawares.
Exodus 34:7 and the high priest's confession use all three main words: every kind of wrong.
Paraptōma is a false step; anomia is lawlessness.
Skopos and telos name the goal: the upward call in Christ, and love from a pure heart.
“Missing the mark” does not make sin minor; it shows how far we fall from the glory we were made for.
Translations rightly use “sin”, but the original pictures help us repent and aim again.
reflect: Which picture describes your own failures best right now: missing, twisting, rebelling or straying?
What is the “target” you are really aiming your life at, and does it match Paul's goal in Philippians 3:14?
How could confessing sin as “we” rather than only “I” change the way your community deals with failure?

quiz.q: In Judges 20:16, what does the Hebrew verb chata describe?
options: A priest who purified the altar
quiz.why: The left-handed slingers of Benjamin could sling a stone at a hair and not chata, “miss”.

quiz.q: Which Hebrew word pictures rebellion or a breach of loyalty?
quiz.why: Pesha is used when Israel “rebelled” against the house of David (1 Kings 12:19).

quiz.q: What does the Greek word skopos mean in Philippians 3:14?
quiz.why: Paul presses on toward the skopos, the goal or mark the runner fixes his eyes on.

quiz.q: How do the ESV and NIV translate 1 John 3:4?
quiz.why: The Greek is anomia, “lawlessness”; the KJV paraphrases it as “the transgression of the law”.

quiz.q: Where does the English word “iniquity” come from?
quiz.why: It comes from Latin iniquitas, “not level”, a good match for avon's picture of crookedness.

terms.def: To miss a target or the way; the most common Hebrew verb for sin.
Iniquity: a twisted act, the guilt it brings, and its consequence.
Rebellion or breach of loyalty against God as King.
An unintentional sin, from shagah, “to stray”.
The ordinary Greek word for sin, from a verb that could mean “to miss”.
A target or goal fixed in view (Philippians 3:14).
End, goal or purpose; the point something aims at.

chapters.title: Tongues
chapters.subtitle: From Babel to Pentecost: one word for the body's tongue and for every language on earth
chapters.trueMeaning: tongue, language: God speaking every people's speech
chapters.nutshell: In Hebrew and Greek the word for the tongue in your mouth is also the word for a language. At Babel God confused the one “lip” of humanity; at Pentecost, the festival Jews linked with the giving of the Torah, the Spirit gave “tongues as of fire” and pilgrims from many nations heard God's mighty works in their own languages. Paul welcomes tongues in Corinth but insists that worship must be understood and must build up the church.
chapters.bigIdea: The gift of tongues shows that God speaks to every nation in its own language and gathers the scattered peoples into one, and it is meant to serve love and understanding in the church.
skeleton: “Speaking in tongues” today raises strong feelings and debates.
Hebrew lashon and safah, and Greek glōssa, mean both the body's tongue or lip and a language.
At Babel one “lip” was confused and the peoples were scattered.
Jewish tradition linked Shavuot with Sinai, and taught that God's voice there went out in the languages of the nations.
At Pentecost pilgrims heard the apostles in their own languages: Babel reversed.
In Corinth Paul values tongues but puts prophecy, interpretation and love first.
Translators added words like “unknown”; Christians still debate what the gift is.
The heart of the gift: God's praise in every language, for building up the church.

p: For some Christians, **speaking in tongues** is a precious part of daily prayer. For others it is a puzzling or even worrying practice they have seen on television. Many assume that the Bible's “tongues” must mean either an unknown heavenly language or a miracle of foreign languages, and churches have argued about it for a long time.

Before we take sides, it helps to hear the words as the first readers heard them. In both Hebrew and Greek, **the same word means the tongue in your mouth and a language**. The story of tongues in the Bible is a story about languages: how humanity was divided by them, and how God speaks through them to gather the nations back to himself.

sections.h: Lashon and safah: tongue and lip
p: The Hebrew word *lashon* means the physical tongue (“my tongue sticks to my jaws”, Psalm 22:15) and also a language. After the flood, the nations were spread out “each with his own language (*lashon*)” (Genesis 10:5). Hebrew uses *lashon* for anything tongue-shaped too: a bar of gold (Joshua 7:21) and a bay of the sea (Isaiah 11:15).

*Safah* means “lip”, and also “edge” or “shore”: the sand on the *sefat ha-yam*, the lip of the sea (Genesis 22:17). It too can mean language. Genesis 11:1 says, “the whole earth had one *safah*”, literally one lip. Later Jews called Hebrew *lashon ha-kodesh*, “the holy tongue”, and the rabbis warned against *lashon hara*, “the evil tongue”, meaning harmful gossip. The tongue is a small organ with great power for good or ill (compare James 3:5–10).

At Babel, people with one language tried to build a tower “with its top in the heavens” and make a name for themselves, so that they would not be scattered (Genesis 11:4). God came down and said, “let us confuse their language (*safah*), so that they may not understand one another's speech” (11:7). The city was called Babel because there the LORD “confused” (*balal*) the language of all the earth, and from there he scattered them (11:9).

The prophets look forward to a reversal. Zephaniah hears God promise: “I will change the speech of the peoples to a pure speech (*safah berurah*), that all of them may call upon the name of the LORD and serve him with one accord” (Zephaniah 3:9). Isaiah warns that God will speak to his stubborn people “by people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue” (Isaiah 28:11), words Paul later quotes about tongues (1 Corinthians 14:21).

sections.h: Shavuot: the festival of the giving of the Torah
p: Pentecost is the Greek name for the Jewish festival of **Shavuot**, “Weeks”, held fifty days after Passover (Leviticus 23:15–16). It was one of the three pilgrim festivals when Jews went up to Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 16:16). The Torah presents it as a harvest feast. Jewish tradition also links it with the giving of the Torah at Sinai, which Exodus 19:1 places in the third month; the Jewish prayer book calls Shavuot “the season of the giving of our Torah”.

At Sinai there were thunder, fire and a great sound (Exodus 19:16–19). Exodus 20:18 says literally that “all the people saw the voices and the torches”. Jewish tradition reflected deeply on that voice. The Talmud records the teaching that every word that went out from God's mouth divided into seventy languages (Talmud Shabbat 88b), seventy being the traditional number of the nations listed in Genesis 10. The Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria also describes the voice at Sinai as a flame that became speech.

> Whatever the exact age of these traditions, they show how Jews could think about Sinai: God's word was meant for every nation, in every language. Luke's account of Pentecost sounds like an answer to that hope.

On the day of Pentecost the disciples were together, and “a sound like a mighty rushing wind” came from heaven, and “divided tongues as of fire” rested on each of them. “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues (*heterais glōssais*) as the Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:2–4).

Jerusalem was full of Jewish pilgrims “from every nation under heaven” (2:5). Luke lists them: Parthians, Medes, Elamites, people from Mesopotamia, Judea, Asia, Egypt, Rome, Crete and Arabia (2:9–11). Each one heard them speaking “in his own language (*dialektos*)” (2:6, 8), telling “the mighty works of God” (2:11). Luke says the crowd was “bewildered” (*synchéō*), the same verb the Greek Genesis uses for God “confusing” the languages at Babel (Genesis 11:7, 9).

At Babel, one language became many, and people were scattered and could not understand each other. At Pentecost, the many languages remained, but **everyone understood**, and the scattered were gathered. God did not make everyone speak Hebrew or Greek; he spoke each people's own language. Later the same gift comes to Gentiles in Cornelius's house (Acts 10:46) and to disciples in Ephesus (Acts 19:6).

In 1 Corinthians 12–14 Paul lists “various kinds of tongues” and “the interpretation of tongues” (*hermēneia*) among the Spirit's gifts (12:10). He speaks of “the tongues of men and of angels” (13:1) and says that one who speaks in a tongue “speaks not to men but to God, for no one understands him; he utters mysteries in the Spirit” (14:2). He thanks God that he speaks in tongues more than all of them (14:18) and says, “do not forbid speaking in tongues” (14:39).

Yet Paul sets clear priorities. Without love, tongues are a noisy gong (13:1). In the assembly, “I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue” (14:19). Only two or three should speak, in turn, and someone must interpret; if there is no interpreter, they should keep silent in church and speak to themselves and to God (14:27–28). Tongues with interpretation can build up the church; everything must be done “decently and in order” (14:40).

The KJV adds the word “unknown” in 1 Corinthians 14 (“he that speaketh in an **unknown** tongue”, 14:2, 4, 13, 14, 19, 27), printing it in italics to show it is not in the Greek. The translators wanted to explain that no one present understood, but the addition decides a question the Greek leaves open. Most modern versions (ESV, NIV, NASB) say simply “in a tongue”.

Translators also have to choose between “tongues” and “languages”. In Acts 2:4 the KJV, ESV and NIV say “other tongues”, while the NLT says “other languages”. “Tongues” keeps the link with the tongues of fire and with Paul's letters, but sounds strange in modern English; “languages” is clear in Acts 2, where people heard their own dialects, but may decide the Corinthian debate in advance. In 1 Corinthians 12–14, the NIV has at times added notes such as “or languages”, which is honest about the choice.

The Septuagint made its own choices. In Genesis 11 it renders Hebrew *safah* (“lip”) with Greek *cheilos*, “lip”, in 11:1, and uses *glōssa* in 11:7. English versions say “language” throughout, which reads naturally but hides the body words. The everyday Hebrew picture is that a people's lips and tongue are its language.

Jews in the first century were a people of many languages. In the land, most spoke Aramaic, read Scripture in Hebrew, and used Greek for trade. In the diaspora, from Babylon to Rome, many spoke only Greek or the local language. In the synagogue, the Hebrew reading was followed by a spoken translation into Aramaic, the *targum*, and the Mishnah rules that the reader must give the translator only one verse at a time from the Torah (Mishnah Megillah 4:4). Interpretation in turn, so that everyone understood, was a normal part of worship.

Corinth was a busy Greek port with many cults. Some Greek religions valued inspired, ecstatic speech: the priestess at Delphi gave oracles, and worshippers of Dionysus sought religious frenzy. Scholars debate how much this background explains the problems in Corinth, but Paul's insistence on order, interpretation and the mind fits a church tempted to treat spiritual excitement as a sign of status. The Greek *hermēneia* (interpretation) is linked in ancient minds with Hermes, the messenger of the gods, and gives us the word “hermeneutics”.

Christians understand this gift in different ways. Pentecostal and charismatic believers usually see tongues as a continuing gift, often a prayer language not learned by study, and sometimes a real human language unknown to the speaker. Others see the tongues in Acts and Corinth as real human languages. Some traditions believe this gift ceased after the apostles, pointing to 1 Corinthians 13:8, “as for tongues, they will cease”; others reply that Paul is speaking of the end of the age.

All sides can agree on what Paul stresses: the gift comes from the Spirit, it is not a mark of spiritual superiority (“do all speak with tongues?”, 12:30), it must serve love, and in the assembly it must be understood so that the church is built up. Christians who disagree can honour one another and stay together on these points.

Pentecost shows God's heart for **every language**. The gospel is not tied to one culture's speech. When the Bible is read, sung and prayed in Tamil, English, Hindi or any other language, the work of Pentecost continues. Honour your own language as a gift to praise God, and honour the languages of others.

Remember too that the tongue in your mouth is a gift. The same tongue that can praise God can wound people with *lashon hara*. Let Zephaniah's “pure lip” describe your speech: words that call on the name of the LORD, serve others, and build up the church in love.

words.note: The body's tongue and a people's language; also a bar of gold or a bay of the sea.
words.missed: English must choose “tongue” or “language”, so the body picture disappears.
words.culture: Jews called Hebrew lashon ha-kodesh, “the holy tongue”, and warned against lashon hara, harmful speech.

words.note: Babel's “one lip” was confused; Zephaniah promises a “pure lip”.
words.missed: “Language” is clear but hides that Hebrew speaks of lips.
words.culture: The same word names the shore of the sea, the lip of the water.

words.note: A wordplay explains the name Babel: there God “confused” the language.
words.missed: Readers of English do not hear the sound-play between Babel and balal.
words.culture: The verb is also used for mixing flour with oil for offerings (Leviticus 2:4).

words.note: Like lashon, both the organ and a language.
words.missed: “Tongues” can sound mysterious in English, though it is the normal word for languages.
words.culture: Greek writers also used glōssa for rare or obscure words, which is why scholars debate its sense in Corinth.

words.note: The phrase behind the later word “glossolalia”.
words.missed: The KJV's added “unknown” in 1 Corinthians 14 decides a question the Greek leaves open.
words.culture: In Acts it happens in Jerusalem, a Gentile home and Ephesus: the gospel crossing every boundary.

words.note: Each pilgrim heard “in his own language”, the one he was born into.
words.missed: Both glōssa and dialektos are often rendered “language”, so the shift between them is hard to see.
words.culture: Paul addressed the Jerusalem crowd “in the Hebrew dialect” (Acts 21:40), and they grew quiet.

words.note: Paul links tongues to Isaiah's warning of foreign speech.
words.missed: Readers may not notice that Paul calls a prophet's words “the Law”, meaning Scripture in general.
words.culture: For Israel, hearing foreign speech was a sign of judgment by invading armies (Deuteronomy 28:49).

words.note: The gift that makes tongues understandable and so able to build up.
words.missed: “Interpretation” can sound like explaining an opinion; it also means translating.
words.culture: Synagogues had a translator (meturgeman) who rendered the Hebrew reading into Aramaic verse by verse.

words.note: The verb links Pentecost's bewildered crowd with Babel's confused languages.
words.missed: English “bewildered” (Acts) and “confuse” (Genesis) hide that Luke echoes the Greek Genesis.
words.culture: Greek-speaking Jews knew their Scriptures in the Septuagint and could hear the echo.

rows.literal: one lip and the same words
rows.common: of one language, and of one speech (KJV)
rows.why: “Language” is the natural English sense, but it hides the Hebrew body word “lip” that Zephaniah later picks up.
Clear English, but the promise of a “purified lip” for the nations echoes Babel's confused lip and points toward Pentecost.
The NLT chooses clarity because the hearers recognised their own languages; “tongues” (KJV, ESV, NIV) keeps the link with the tongues of fire.

rows.literal: for the one speaking in a tongue
rows.common: he that speaketh in an unknown tongue (KJV)
rows.why: The KJV added “unknown”, marked in italics, to explain the verse; it leaves out of view the question of whether a human language was meant.

rows.original: ἐν ἑτερογλώσσοις καὶ ἐν χείλεσιν ἑτέρων
rows.literal: by people of other tongues and by the lips of others
rows.common: With men of other tongues and other lips (KJV)
rows.why: Here the KJV keeps both body words, tongues and lips, which link Paul's quotation to Isaiah and Babel.

events.d: The peoples spread “each with his own tongue”; at Babel God confuses their one lip.
Fire, sound and voices; later Jewish tradition says God's word went out in seventy languages.
God will give the peoples a pure lip to call on his name together.
Tongues of fire; pilgrims from many nations hear God's works in their own languages.
The Spirit and tongues come to Cornelius's household and to disciples in Ephesus.
Tongues with interpretation, prophecy and above all love build up the church.

verses.text: Now the whole earth had one language and the same words.
Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth.
At that time I will change the speech of the peoples to a pure speech, that all of them may call upon the name of the LORD.
They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.
We hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.
If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal.
In church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.

keyPoints: Hebrew lashon and safah and Greek glōssa mean both a body part (tongue, lip) and a language.
At Babel God confused humanity's one “lip” and scattered the nations.
Shavuot (Pentecost) was linked in Jewish tradition with the giving of the Torah; the Talmud tells of God's word going out in seventy languages.
At Pentecost the many languages remained but everyone understood: Babel reversed and the scattered gathered.
Paul values tongues but puts love, understanding, interpretation and building up the church first.
The KJV's italic “unknown” in 1 Corinthians 14 is an addition; Christians still debate what the gift is.
God speaks every people's language; the gospel belongs to every tongue.
reflect: What does it mean to you that God chose to speak the pilgrims' own languages rather than one holy language?
How can your church make sure that what is said in worship is understood and builds people up?
Is your tongue more often used for blessing or for lashon hara? What would a “pure lip” look like for you this week?

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew word safah literally mean in Genesis 11:1?
quiz.why: Safah means lip (and edge or shore); “one lip” means one language.
Pentecost (“fiftieth”) is Shavuot, held fifty days after Passover, which Jewish tradition links with the giving of the Torah.

quiz.q: What did the pilgrims in Acts 2 hear?
options: God's mighty works in their own languages
quiz.why: Each heard “in his own language” the mighty works of God (Acts 2:6–11).

quiz.q: In 1 Corinthians 14:2, where does the KJV's word “unknown” come from?
options: It is in the Greek text
The translators added it in italics
It is from the Vulgate only
quiz.why: The KJV printed “unknown” in italics to show it was added for explanation.

quiz.q: What does Paul say must happen if someone speaks in a tongue in the assembly?
options: The speaker must stand on a platform
quiz.why: Two or three in turn, with interpretation; otherwise they keep silent and speak to God (1 Corinthians 14:27–28).

terms.def: Hebrew for tongue and language.
Hebrew for lip, edge or shore, and language.
Greek for tongue and language; behind “speaking in tongues”.
The Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover; in Greek, Pentecost.
Interpretation or translation; the gift that makes tongues understood.
An Aramaic translation of Scripture read aloud in the synagogue.
“The evil tongue”: rabbinic term for harmful gossip and slander.
